why:
phase-430 W4 -- the clock axis on the DECLARATIVE surface, and the sibling of `rust:DeclaredNode::create_timer_for_callback_name` directly above: same declarative model (entities are declared by a component, RFC-0043/0044), one argument more.

Filed `divergence` and not `extension` because rclrs HAS the capability: a per-timer clock, expressed as a per-site OPTION (`IntoTimerOptions::{clock, node_time, steady_time, system_time}` on `Node::create_timer_repeating`, all `declined` in this shard) rather than as a second verb. What differs is the shape, and the same constraint that decided `rust:Executor::register_timer_on_clock` decides it here: a non-`Steady` timer READS a clock on every poll, which on an RTOS target is a platform call, so it is worth a distinct name at the call site rather than a default inside an options builder.

Why it exists at all: until W4 the clock reached only the executor, so a component -- which is how every workspace example writes a timer -- could not ask for one without reaching past its own API. `EntityMetadata::timer_clock` carries the choice to `node_runtime`, which registers through the one dispatch, `Executor::register_timer_on_clock`. The `#[doc(hidden)]` `create_timer_on_clock` / `create_timer_for_callback_on_clock` beneath it are the same verb with the entity ID spelled explicitly, as for the clock-less trio.

phase-483 W3 — re-keyed from `DeclaredNode`: the declarative constructors are now the `nros::DeclarativeNode` extension trait on `nros::Node`, so a component's node and a program's node are one type.

Issue 2038 (2026-10-25, resolved): the declarative surface has the call info (`CallbackCtx::timer_info`) and the autostart flag (`create_timer_for_callback_name_with_autostart`, this verb plus one `bool`). See `rust:DeclarativeNode::create_timer_for_callback_name`.
